sections.h2: Where do I pay and ask questions about a Wabasha County tax bill?
sections.html:
Take the bill to the Auditor/Treasurer's office at 625 Jefferson Avenue in the city of Wabasha, open weekdays from eight in the morning to four in the afternoon. The Assessor works from the same address and handles questions about value and classification at 651-565-3669. A copy of a statement can be requested at 651-565-2648, and the county's statement page links to an online Beacon search that asks for a parcel number or an address.

The Auditor/Treasurer's payment page lists these ways to pay:

  • Online at www.co.wabasha.mn.us/paytax, or by phone at 1-866-539-2020 (bureau code 8190128) from 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. on weekdays, with the parcel number and amount ready; the processor adds a convenience fee
  • Direct Payment Plan (ACH) covering real estate and personal property taxes, with forms at the office or through 651-565-4410
  • The brown drop box in front of the courthouse
  • Mail with the payment stub, carrying an official postmark dated no later than the due date
  • In person with cash, check, money order, e-check, credit card or debit card

A change of address matters here. Returned statements and notices come back to the county, so tell the office even if the move is temporary.

sections.h2: What is Wabasha County like for someone selling a house?
sections.html:
Wabasha County runs along the Mississippi River in southeastern Minnesota, with part of Lake Pepin on its shoreline. The territorial legislature created it on October 27, 1849, as one of nine original counties, and its lines have stayed the same since 1855. The city of Wabasha is the county seat, while Lake City, which spills into Goodhue County, is the largest city. Other cities include Plainview, Mazeppa, Elgin, Kellogg, Hammond, Millville, Zumbro Falls, Bellechester and Minneiska.

The land is low rolling hills cut by drainages, with the Zumbro and Whitewater rivers crossing it and Carley State Park among the protected areas. The county is part of the Rochester metropolitan area, yet the 2020 census counted 81.2% of residents as rural. Census QuickFacts gives this picture:

  • 21,537 residents in July 2025, a gain of 0.8% over the 2020 base
  • 10,439 housing units, 83.3% of them owner-occupied
  • Median owner-occupied value of $264,400, with monthly owner costs of $1,763 for those carrying a mortgage
  • Median gross rent of $830 and median household income of $82,007
  • 51 building permits in 2025, and 25.4% of residents aged 65 or older

With very few new homes going up and an older population, many sales here involve an inherited farmhouse, a retiree's downsizing or a house that sat empty after a move. In each case the tax picture is settled by the Auditor/Treasurer before a deed can be recorded.

sections.h2: When are Wabasha County property taxes due?
sections.html:
Most real estate is payable in two halves, and the county notes that a due date landing on a weekend slides to the following Monday. November 15 is a Sunday in 2026, so second-half payments for agricultural land and mobile homes are due Monday, November 16. The October 15 date for ordinary real estate has already passed.

Wabasha County payment dates from the Auditor/Treasurer's statement page
Type of propertyFirst paymentSecond payment
Real estate, most classesMay 15October 15
Classified agriculturalMay 15November 15
Mobile (manufactured) homesAugust 31November 15
Unpaid prior-year taxBecomes delinquent January 2

Statements go out at the end of March. Mobile home statements follow later, with the assessor's calendar giving July 15 as the mailing deadline. A buyer who closes after the mailing does not get a statement from the county. The office sends a courtesy letter showing the year's tax instead, even when a lender pays from escrow.

sections.h2: What does a late payment cost in Wabasha County?
sections.html:
Under Minnesota Statutes 279.01, an unpaid installment picks up 2% on homestead property or 4% on non-homestead property the day after it is due. The same amount is added again on the first of the next month, then 1% more each month, up to 8% for homestead and 12% for non-homestead. The back of your statement carries the county's own table.

The county's FAQ is blunt that penalties are not waived, because the rates come from state law. Wabasha County mails a courtesy notice a couple of weeks after a missed date showing the tax and the penalty so far. The statute does give one relief: if the envelope is postmarked within one business day of the deadline, the treasurer must abate the penalty, though only for an owner who has not used that relief before. Unpaid tax turns delinquent on January 2, and a delinquent balance follows the parcel into any sale.

sections.h2: How do I contest a Wabasha County valuation?
sections.html:
The assessment date is January 2. Market value notices arrive between March and May, at least 10 days before the local board of appeal and equalization meets, and those local boards sit between April 1 and May 31. Start with the assessor, since questions about a changed value or a switch from homestead to non-homestead go to 651-565-3669.

  1. Meet your local board if your city or township holds one, bringing an appraisal or comparable sales.
  2. Take the dispute up to the county-level board of appeal and equalization, which convenes during the last 10 meeting days of June after the second Friday. Times are printed on the valuation notice.
  3. Or petition the Minnesota Tax Court. April 30 is the last day to file a petition about current taxes, and under section 278.01 a copy must be served on the county auditor.

For mobile homes taxed as personal property, the county calendar sets September 1 as the deadline for a Tax Court petition on valuation.

sections.h2: How does a Wabasha County sale deal with the tax bill?
sections.html:
Before a deed is recorded, the auditor checks the records for delinquent tax. Section 272.12 says the recorder must refuse the document unless it carries the notation that no delinquent taxes are due. Back taxes therefore have to be cleared at or before the closing table. Call the Auditor/Treasurer at 651-565-2648 for the current balance while the closing date is still open.

How the current year is split between seller and buyer is a matter for the purchase agreement and the closing statement, so confirm that with the title company or attorney handling the sale. Heirs selling a parent's house should also remember that tax statements follow the mailing address on file, and the county asks owners to report moves because undeliverable mail is returned to its office.

sections.h2: Which other Wabasha County tax deadlines should a homeowner know?
sections.html:
The assessor's important dates page lists several filing dates that sit outside the two payments:

  • February 1: last day to file an exemption from taxation with the assessor
  • May 1: Green Acres deferment applications for the following year's taxes
  • July 1: disabled veterans homestead market value exclusion applications, and the senior citizen deferral filing
  • August 15: Property Tax Refund (form M-1PR)
  • October 1: special homestead classification for people who are blind or permanently and totally disabled
  • December 31: last day to establish homestead for the current year's assessment

Proposed-tax (Truth in Taxation) notices are due out by November 24, and local taxing bodies hold budget hearings between November 29 and December 20. Those hearings are the moment to speak about next year's levy.

faqs.q: What is the next Wabasha County property tax deadline?
faqs.a: Monday, November 16, 2026 for classified agricultural land and mobile home second halves, because November 15 is a Sunday. Ordinary real estate had its second-half date on October 15, which has passed, so call 651-565-2648 about any balance.

faqs.q: Will I receive a tax statement if I buy a Wabasha County house in summer?
faqs.a: No. The county sends a courtesy letter showing the year's tax instead, even when your lender escrows the payment. Check the amount with the Auditor/Treasurer so the bill does not go unpaid.

faqs.q: Can Wabasha County waive my late penalty?
faqs.a: Generally no, since the county says state statute sets the rates. The one statutory exception is a payment mailed with a postmark within one business day of the due date, which is abated for an owner who has not used that relief before.

faqs.q: Who explains a change in my Wabasha County value or classification?
faqs.a: The county Assessor at 651-565-3669. The office is at 625 Jefferson Avenue in Wabasha and keeps weekday hours until four in the afternoon. Bring an appraisal or recent comparable sales if you plan to appeal.

faqs.q: What is the last day to take a Wabasha County valuation dispute to Tax Court?
faqs.a: April 30 of the year the tax is payable. Serve the petition on the county auditor and file it with the court administrator by then. Mobile homes assessed as personal property have a separate deadline of September 1.
